extracted.intended_audience: actors, stage people, journalists, public speakers, and writers of memoirs; general readers interested in theatrical and literary craft
extracted.subtask_description: Memoir-essay offering evaluative observations and practical guidance about acting, stagecraft, public speaking/lecturing, and the writing of memoirs, illustrated by examples from Joseph Jefferson and others. Focuses on qualities that make performance and personal narrative effective and respectable.

rubrics_metrics.name: simulate_not_experience_emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor 'must simulate, not experience emotion; the effect [should be] referable to the seeming, never to the actuality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: an actor 'broke down' in performance (Jefferson as Caleb Plummer), spoiling the scene; maintain artful control so tears/cues are rendered by technique rather than genuine collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: self_possession_and_control
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor 'must be master of himself, holding the situation and his art by the firmest grip.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve composure onstage and off; self-possession enables consistent performance and prevents lapses under unexpected pressures (e.g., being put on the spot at a dinner or by stage mishaps).

rubrics_metrics.name: wit_must_exceed_dirt
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid salacious material unless the wit outweighs the dirt: 'the wit must exceed the dirt; where the dirt exceeded the wit we would none of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refuse material that panders to salacity without sufficient cleverness; prefer refined humor over coarse or gratuitously lewd content.

rubrics_metrics.name: clean_speech_no_profanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Jefferson's speech exemplified clean language: 'Cleaner speech never fell from the lips of man. I never heard him use a profanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid profanity in public performance and personal reputation; clean diction contributes to moral sensibility and broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_personal_displays_or_gagging
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor 'shrank from personal displays of every sort' and 'rarely "gagged," or interpolated, upon the stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not trade on off-stage personality or improvisational 'gags' that break character or self-effacement; keep private entertainments distinct from public performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: versatility_over_one_part
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective actor 'possessed uncommon versatility' and was not just a 'one-part actor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a range of parts and styles (comic, tragic, serio-comic, etc.); repeatedly succeeding in a single famous role should not be mistaken for incapacity to vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: self_effacing_purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor's purpose is 'to fill the scene and forget himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the integrity of the role and the scene over ego or seeking personal display; effective acting is self-effacing and service-oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: cultivate_voice_and_stage_speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Good stage voice and speaking: Jefferson 'was always a good stage speaker' with tones 'soft and liquid' retaining lasting charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train vocal qualities and musical sensibility; singing, rhythm, and tonal control enrich stage presence and expressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: stage_manager_character_and_treatment_of_company
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful theatrical leader is 'a thorough stage manager, skillful, patient and upright. His company was his family.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage with fairness and patience; treat company members as a family—train and protect young performers, maintain professionalism and moral standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: elevate_social_and_intellectual_standing_of_stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of an actor's success is to 'elevate the personality, the social and intellectual standing of the actor and the stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue roles, manners, and public conduct that raise the theater's respectability; actions that improve public and clerical attitudes toward the stage count as significant contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: memoirs_should_avoid_trivial_gossip
rubrics_metrics.description: Memoirs of the 'trivial French School or gossiping letters and diaries' are 'an unprofitable task' for great men; many immoderate autobiographies excite no special interest when badly timed or trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write memoirs only when you have substantial, interesting material or insight; avoid mere gossip and ephemeral scandal—aim for narrative value and lasting interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: memoirs_should_address_key_contested_facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A memoir ought to illuminate the important contested episodes of a life: 'The single chapter in his life on which light was desirable was the military episode... Fuller, more convincing vindication could not be asked of any man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use memoir to clarify, vindicate, or explain crucial episodes that shaped reputation or public controversy; factual, convincing exposition strengthens a memoir's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: timing_and_relevance_of_publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Delayed publication or ill-timed memoirs may 'excite no especial interest' and 'lie dusty upon the shelves' (Talleyrand example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider timing, audience appetite, and relevance when publishing memoirs; excessive postponement or overlong secrecy can blunt impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: adapt_existing_material_with_framing_for_new_occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: When pressed for time, adapt an existing lecture by adding 'a foreword and a few words in conclusion' to meet a new occasion or thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatic technique for public speaking: reframe and stitch preexisting material to fit a different debate or audience without inventing wholly new content.

rubrics_metrics.name: inclusive_rhetoric_for_persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective oratory may universalize (e.g., 'We are all workingmen') to broaden appeal and neutralize class-exclusive claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inclusive formulations to connect diverse audiences and undercut divisive labels in persuasive speeches; rhetorical universality can disarm partisan expectations.
